entities.name: The Military & Technical Corpus (Early)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Military & Technical Corpus (Early) encompasses the treatises, manuals, and technical literature on warfare, fortification, siege engineering, military organization, and weapons technology from antiquity through the early modern period (c. 500 BCE – 1700 CE). This corpus traces one of the most consequential threads in human history: how the technology of organized violence co-evolved with state formation, engineering innovation, and scientific inquiry.

Key classical works include: Vegetius's Epitoma Rei Militaris (De Re Militari, late 4th century CE) — the most influential military treatise in Western history, read continuously for 1,500 years and consulted by every major European commander from Charlemagne to Napoleon; Vitruvius's De Architectura (c. 30–15 BCE) — the only surviving classical architectural-engineering treatise, covering siege engines, water supply, astronomy, and fortress design; Aeneas Tacticus's How to Survive Under Siege (c.

360 BCE) — the earliest surviving Western military manual; and Frontinus's Strategemata. Medieval and early modern works include: Byzantine military manuals (the Sylloge Tacticorum, 10th century; the treatise on Greek Fire — the Byzantine Empire's superweapon); Chinese military texts (Sun Tzu's Art of War, c. 5th century BCE; the Wujing Zongyao, 1044 CE — first documented gunpowder formulas); the Codex Atlanticus of Leonardo da Vinci (drawings of flying machines, tanks, bridges, and fortifications); and Niccolò Tartaglia's Nova Scientia (1537) — the first mathematical analysis of ballistics. This corpus documents the fateful marriage of science and warfare that transformed the world.
